newsitem.title: POLAND: China seeks couple's extradition from Poland.
newsitem.headline: China seeks couple's extradition from Poland.

text.p: Polish human rights activists are battling to prevent the extradition of two members of China's Mongolian minority, wanted by Beijing on fraud and other charges which they say could incur the death penalty.

Mandugeqi, 52, and his 42-year-old wife Yinge were detained during a visit to Warsaw in August on the basis of an Interpol notice and have since been held in separate jails pending a decision on whether to grant China's request for extradition.

"If extradited they would risk, if not the death penalty then long years in a labour camp which in practice would mean the same as a death sentence," Wojciech Hermelinski, a lawyer representing the couple on behalf of the Polish Helsinki Committee, said on Friday.
He told Reuters the Warsaw prosecutor's office had sent a motion to the provincial court asking it to give an opinion on China's request and the court was to examine it on Monday.
Chinese authorities issued an arrest warrant in 1994, the year after the couple left the country.

Hermelinski said the pair faced imprecisely-formulated allegations of fraud, failing to repay borrowed money from banks and individuals and of not paying for goods, together involving a total of about 17.5 million yuan ($2.1 million).
The couple argue they repaid practically all they owed and assets they left in China covered any outstanding sums.
Hermelinski said the extradition should not go through as the allegations would not be treated in Poland as a criminal matter but as an issue for civil proceedings, he said.
The couple, who have recently been living in Mongolia, argue that they had to leave China in 1993 because they learned they were wanted because of Mandugeqi's political activities.

Hermelinski said they had evidence Mandugeqi had been sentenced to eight years in jail in 1964 on charges of wanting to cross the border into Mongolia and preparing a map and that he belonged to an organisation based in Ulan Bator campaigning among other things for the rights of Mongolians in China.
Poland and China have no extradition treaty although Warsaw's Justice Minister Leszek Kubicki suggested during a visit to Beijing this month that there should be one.

Poland's top-selling daily Gazeta Wyborcza, which has been campaigning on behalf of the couple, said this week that the prosecutor's office had proposed that China should be asked to agree to three conditions if the extradition was approved.

China should undertake that they would not be sentenced to death, that they would only have to face the charges stipulated and that any penalties imposed should not exceed those they might have faced for such offences under Polish laws.
But the lawyer argued that Poland could not ensure that China would honour such an undertaking, saying a similar Chinese promise in the past, to Thailand, had been broken.
China applies death and other harsh penalties to a wide range of crimes and Hermelinski said that to extradite the pair would infringe the European Convention on Human Rights.
The prosecutor's office declined to comment before the court hearing.
If the Warsaw court decides extradition is justified, the decision can be appealed and would eventually rest with Kubicki as prosecutor-general.
